rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites claim one grave sin may outweigh decades of sincere obedience because God's immense gifts make disobedience exceptionally grave; al-Rāzī rejects this as irrationally unjust.
rows.anchor: قال الجبائي : إنه لا يمتنع أن تكون الكبيرة الواحدة أعظم من كل طاعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī argues that one hour of faith can erase seventy years of unbelief, so reason likewise resists saying one hour of sin erases seventy years of faith.
rows.anchor: إيمان ساعة يهدم كفر سبعين سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command may prohibit charity that was invalid from the outset through ostentation, which does not support the Muʿtazilite doctrine of later cancellation.
rows.anchor: وذلك أن ينوي بالصدقة الرياء والسمعة

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites read the smooth stone and rain as charity that first earned reward, then lost it through reproach and injury.
rows.anchor: فهذا يشهد لتأويلهم ، لأنه تعالى جعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī reads the ostentatious unbeliever as a deed invalid from inception; the dust is the outward charitable act, only apparently attached to the smooth stone, like charity with corrupt intent.
rows.anchor: لا نسلم أن المشبه بوقوع الغبار على الصفوان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says reproach is toward God for the gift and injury toward the petitioner; al-Rāzī finds this possible but says the other view is clearer.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما : لا تبطلوا صدقاتكم بالمن على الله

rows.speaker: الباقون
rows.claim: The other authorities take reproach and injury as directed toward the poor recipient; al-Rāzī considers this the clearer reading.
rows.anchor: وقال الباقون : بالمن على الفقير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first parsing makes the comparison an ellipsis for invalidating charity like the ostentatious person's; both acts lack God's pleasure, supporting invalidity from the outset.
rows.anchor: قولان الأول : أنه متعلق بمحذوف والتقدير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second parsing makes the comparison an accusative of state: donors must not invalidate charity while resembling someone who gives to be seen.
rows.anchor: والقول الثاني : أن يكون الكاف في محل النصب على الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Riyāʾ is the verbal noun for showing one's deed to another person, with forms compared to other Arabic verbal nouns.
rows.anchor: الرياء مصدر ، كالمراءاة يقال : راأيته رياء ومراءاة

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayd transmits al-Aṣmaʿī's view that ṣafwān, ṣafā, and ṣafwā are equivalent names for a smooth stone; al-Rāzī also defines wابل and صلد as heavy rain and barren, smooth stone.
rows.anchor: وحكى أبو عبيد عن الأصمعي أن الصفوان والصفا والصفوا واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable shows that reproachers, injurers, and hypocrites seem to have deeds, but at Resurrection their work vanishes because it was never done for God.
rows.anchor: فإذا كان يوم القيامة اضمحل كله وبطل لأنه تبين أن تلك الأعمال ما كانت لله تعالى

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites instead say the charity first earned reward and reproach and injury later removed it, as rain removes dust from stone.
rows.anchor: وأما المعتزلة فقالوا : إن المعنى أن تلك الصدقة أوجبت الأجر والثواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī maps outward work to dust, the hypocrite or reproaching donor to the stone, and Judgment Day to rain; the rival reading maps reproach to rain.
rows.anchor: الأول : ما ذكرنا أن العمل الظاهر كالتراب

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffāl offers a seed analogy: sincere deeds grow like seed in fertile garden soil, while the reproacher's deed is seed stored on sterile stone and yields nothing when needed.
rows.anchor: قال القفال رحمه الله تعالى ، وفيه احتمال آخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In reply to the objection that rain cleans stone, al-Rāzī says only the stated likeness matters; al-Qāḍī adds benefits of dust, but al-Rāzī relies on his first explanation.
rows.anchor: والجواب أن وجه التشبيه ما ذكرناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading of the pronoun says no one can recover the seed once the dust washes away, supporting al-Qaffāl's interpretation that the deed cannot benefit its giver.
rows.anchor: أحدهما : أنه عائد إلى معلوم غير مذكور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reading refers the pronoun to the ostentatious spender, with the generic expression functioning as a general class.
rows.anchor: والثاني : أنه عائد إلى قوله { كالذي ينفق ماله }

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffāl gives a third reading: the words return to the believers addressed by the command, shifting from direct address to third person as in Yūnus 10:22.
rows.anchor: قال القفال رحمه الله : وفيه وجه ثالث

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: On the Muʿtazilite account, God does not guide disbelievers by leading them away from reward and Paradise because of their own choices; another view glosses this as removal of faith.
rows.anchor: على قول المعتزلة : إنه تعالى يضلهم عن الثواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrasting sincere donors spend for two ends: seeking God's pleasure and تثبيت of themselves.
rows.anchor: غرض هؤلاء المنفقين من هذا الانفاق أمران

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qāḍī says تثبيت means training oneself to preserve obedience and avoid what corrupts it, including subsequent reproach and injury.
rows.anchor: يوطنون أنفسهم على حفظ هذه الطاعة وترك ما يفسدها

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid's reading, وتثبيتا من بعض أنفسهم, supports construing تثبيت as reassuring others that the donors' faith and sincerity are genuine.
rows.anchor: ويعضده قراءة مجاهد { وتثبيتا من * بعض * أنفسهم }

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: The Kashshāf explains that struggle subdues part of the self attached to worldly life and wealth; spending money stabilizes part, while spending life stabilizes all, as in al-Ṣaff 61:11.
rows.anchor: ومعشوقها أمران : الحياة العاجلة والمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī proposes that the heart becomes firm through God's remembrance; spending brings calm only when done solely for worship, illustrated by ʿAlī's words in al-Insān 76:9.
rows.anchor: أن ثبات القلب لا يحصل إلا بذكر الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He also cites the report about Abū Bakr's spending as seeking only God's face, and notes the rational principle that repeating acts produces stable dispositions.
rows.anchor: ووصف إنفاق أبي بكر فقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeated giving for God's pleasure creates a lasting disposition: even an accidental lapse quickly returns the heart toward the sacred, spiritually aligning the person with angelic and holy realities.
rows.anchor: صيرورة هذا الابتغاء والطلب ملكة مستقرة في النفس

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says تثبيت is confident assurance that God will not waste or disappoint the donors' work, unlike the hypocrite who sees giving as wasted without belief in reward.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : المراد من التثبيت أنهم ينفقونها

rows.speaker: الحسن ومجاهد وعطاء
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, and ʿAṭāʾ interpret تثبيت as careful placement of alms among people of integrity; al-Ḥasan says a donor gives when the motive is truly for God.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن ومجاهد وعطاء : المراد أن المنفق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ربوة means elevated, swelling ground; the author favors fertile soil that rises and grows with rain over interpreters' ordinary hill, citing Q 22:5 and the contrast with sterile stone.
rows.anchor: وأصلها من قولهم : ربا الشيء يربو إذا ازداد وارتفع

rows.speaker: عاصم وابن عامر
rows.claim: ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir read ربوة with fatḥa on rāʾ, a Tamīm dialect; the other readers use ḍamma, the more common Qurashī form, among seven variants.
rows.anchor: قرأ عاصم وابن عامر { بربوة } بفتح الراء

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes say a garden on a hill yields better, but al-Rāzī objects that elevation or a valley each has disadvantages and prefers fertile swelling soil, supported by Q 22:5 and the stone contrast.
rows.anchor: البستان إذا كان في ربوة من الأرض كان أحسن وأكثر ريعا

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, and Abū ʿAmr lighten أكلها; the remaining readers intensify it. The word means edible fruit or produce, as in Ibrāhīm 14:25, with lexical poetry cited.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو { أكلها } بالتخفيف

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj reads ضعفين as twice as much; ʿAṭāʾ says a single year's yield equals another garden's two-year yield, while al-Aṣamm and Abū Muslim give related doubled-yield readings.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : { اتت أكلها * ضعفين } يعني مثلين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭall is light rain. Either a fertile garden preserves its full yield despite receiving only light rain, or it still yields some fruit; sincere giving is never wasted, little or much.
rows.anchor: الطل : مطر صغير الفطر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sees the amount and manner of spending and its motives, then recompenses each person accordingly, for good with good and evil with evil.
rows.anchor: هو تعالى عالم بكمية النفقات وكيفيتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The garden parable depicts a person who is old, unable to earn, and responsible for helpless dependents; losing the garden to a fiery whirlwind leaves desperate need and regret, like a deed nullified by reproach at Judgment.
rows.anchor: فإذا أصبح الإنسان وشاهد تلك الجنة محرقة بالكلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wudd means complete love; the interrogative is repudiative, and the verse uses it because the desire to avoid such calamity would be maximally intense.
rows.anchor: المسألة الأولى : الود ، هو المحبة الكاملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The garden's palms and grapes are singled out as noble, attractive fruits; rivers and every kind of produce complete a garden of unsurpassable beauty and usefulness.
rows.anchor: وإنما خص النخيل والأعناب بالذكر لأنهما أشرف الفواكه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Old age increases needs while reducing earning capacity, and young children add dependency; the waw before أصابه is circumstantial per al-Kashshāf or semantically conditional per al-Farrāʾ.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) { * الواو } للحال لا للعطف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An iʿṣār is a very strong whirlwind rising and rotating skyward like a column, called a whirlwind locally; an unnamed poet's line confirms the image.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول شاعر : إن كنت ريحا فقد لاقيت إعصارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The burned garden represents ostensibly good acts done without God's pleasure or with corrupting additions; at Judgment their needy owner discovers the acts cannot help, as in al-Zumar 39:47 and al-Furqān 25:23.
rows.anchor: ونظير هذه الآية قوله تعالى : { وبدا لهم من الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Just as God explains these signs with encouragement and warning, He explains signs across religion so people may reflect.
rows.anchor: ترغيبا وترهيبا كذلك يبين الله لكم آياته ودلائله في سائر أمور الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī notes that لعل is a particle of hope inappropriate to God and reports the Muʿtazilite argument that the verse implies God intended all people to believe.
rows.anchor: المسألة الأولى : أن : لعل ، للترجي وهو لا يليق بالله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding passage distinguished spending followed by reproach from sincere spending and supplied each type a clarifying parable; this verse specifies what kind of wealth to give.
rows.anchor: إعلم أنه تعالى رغب في الإنفاق

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan takes the command to spend good things as obligatory alms; he argues that the imperative's apparent force is obligation.
rows.anchor: فقال الحسن : / المراد منه الزكاة المفروضة

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some authorities take the command as voluntary charity, citing reports of people donating their poorest produce and the revelation that followed.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم : المراد منه التطوع

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب والحسن ومجاهد
rows.claim: Reports say ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, and Mujāhid observed people giving inferior fruit and poor property as charity, prompting the verse.
rows.anchor: ما روي عن علي بن أبي طالب كرم الله وجهه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that a man brought a bunch of spoiled dates for charity and the Prophet condemned the act before this verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما : جاء رجل ذات يوم بعذق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says the command can cover both obligatory and voluntary giving because its wording urges action without specifying whether omission is permissible.
rows.anchor: إن المفهوم من الأمر ترجيح جانب الفعل على جانب الترك

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: If the command is obligatory, its general wording supports zakāt on all acquired assets and all crops, even small amounts; opponents restrict crops by reports excluding vegetables and yields below five wasqs.
rows.anchor: ظاهر الآية يدل على وجوب الزكاة في كل مال يكتسبه الإنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view takes ṭayyib as good-quality property and khabīth as inferior property; another, held by Ibn Masʿūd and Mujāhid, takes them as lawful and unlawful.
rows.anchor: والقول الثاني : وهو قول ابن مسعود ومجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revelation context of people giving inferior goods supports the quality reading; moreover, unlawful property cannot normally be accepted even with indulgence, which challenges the lawful/unlawful reading.
rows.anchor: إنا ذكرنا في سبب النزول أنهم يتصدقون برديء أموالهم فنزلت الآية

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffāl answers that إغماض can mean leniency: the verse describes people willing to accept knowingly unlawful property by overlooking its source.
rows.anchor: قال القفال رحمه الله : ويمكن أن يجاب عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Q 3:92 supports reading ṭayyib as valuable goods one likes to own, rather than worthless items one is eager to discard.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى : { لن تنالوا البر حتى * تنفقون * مما تحبون }

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qāḍī argues quality alone cannot be intended, since that would require giving good property even if unlawful; he infers that ṭayyib means lawful.
rows.anchor: واحتج القاضي للقول الثاني فقال : أجمعنا على أن المراد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī proposes ṭayyib can convey both lawful and high quality through the shared idea of being agreeable to reason and religion or to inclination and desire.
rows.anchor: يمكن أن يذكر فيه قول ثالث وهو أن المراد من الطيب هاهنا ما يكون طيبا من كل الوجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For zakāt, all-good or all-poor holdings yield the corresponding share, while mixed holdings require a middle quality; the Prophet told Muʿādh not to take the best assets. Voluntary giving should be from one's best.
rows.anchor: وأما إن كان المال مختلطا فالواجب هو الوسط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī asks what benefit the preposition min adds before the phrase about produce from the earth.
rows.anchor: بقي في الآية سؤال واحد ، وهو أن يقال ما الفائدة في كلمة { من }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ammamtuhu, yammamtuhu, and taʾammamtuhu all mean to aim at something; al-Aʿshā's verse illustrates the verb تيمم.
rows.anchor: يقال : أممته ، ويممته ، وتأممته ، كله

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr doubles the tāʾ in تيمموا by assimilating the two original tāʾs; the other readers pronounce it lightly, with analogous variation elsewhere.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير وحده { ولا تيمموا } بتشديد التاء

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī rejects this assimilation because a doubled initial consonant would require a wasl hamza, which is not used with the present tense.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي : هذا الإدغام غير جائز

rows.speaker: سيبويه والفراء
rows.claim: Authorities disagree about which tāʾ is deleted in the common light reading: Sībawayh says the second; al-Farrāʾ says either may be dropped because the remaining one represents it.
rows.anchor: اختلفوا في التاء المحذوفة على قراءة العامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One syntax ends the clause after ولا تيمموا الخبيث and makes منه تنفقون a rhetorical question; another leaves the clause open and supplies an omitted relative pronoun, as in al-Baqara 2:256.
rows.anchor: وجهين الأول : أنه تم الكلام عند قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: إغماض literally means lowering or closing the eyes and is related to something hidden or subtle, such as obscure speech or a low-lying place.
rows.anchor: الإغماض في اللغة غض البصر ، وإطباق جفن على جفن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation is accepting inferior goods only by lenience or embarrassment, as when a person closes his eyes to what he dislikes; the verse asks why donors offer God what they would not accept.
rows.anchor: أن المراد بالإغماض هاهنا المساهلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes the donor compel the seller to close his eyes, meaning lower the price before the donor would accept the goods.
rows.anchor: والمعنى ولستم بآخذيه إلا إذا أغمضتم بصر البائع يعني أمرتموه بالإغماض والحط من الثمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God needs no charity and is praised for explaining; alternatively, غني warns against giving inferior goods and حميد means He praises good deeds, as in Q 21:94.
rows.anchor: غني عن صدقاتكم ، ومعنى حميد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Satan who promises poverty may be Iblīs, all devils, devils among jinn and humans, or the lower self commanding evil.
rows.anchor: اختلفوا في الشيطان فقيل إبليس وقيل سائر الشياطين وقيل شياطين الجن والإنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Promise can describe good or evil; calling punishment a promise may be ironic, like announcing painful punishment as glad tidings.
rows.anchor: الوعد يستعمل في الخير والشر ، قال الله تعالى : { النار وعدها الله الذين كفروا }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faqr and faqr are two forms for poverty; its root is breaking the backbone, illustrated by Ṭarafa's line, and al-Kashshāf notes two vocalized readings.
rows.anchor: الفقر والفقر لغتان ، وهو الضعيف بسبب قلة المال

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reports that Satan whispers an evil promise while an angel whispers good; the hearer should recognize the source, seek God's protection, and he recited this verse.
rows.anchor: روي عن ابن مسعود رضي الله عنه : إن للشيطان لمة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan transmits an emigrant's advice: a person can locate Satan's influence by noticing where he feels an urge to do wrong.
rows.anchor: وروى الحسن ، قال بعض المهاجرين : من سره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation of الفحشاء is miserliness: Satan first frightens people with poverty because stinginess is universally despised, then urges them to withhold charity and obligations; Ṭarafa's verse uses فاحش for miser.
rows.anchor: الأول : أن الفحشاء هي البخل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reading of الفحشاء is escalation into all wrongdoing: fear of poverty first stops quality giving, then all charity and obligatory duties, numbing conscience until further sins become easy.
rows.anchor: فإذا أطاع الرجل الشيطان في ذلك زاد الشيطان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Generosity is the virtuous extreme of giving all; refusing all is the deficient extreme, while withholding quality goods but giving poor goods is the middle step by which Satan draws a person toward total refusal.
rows.anchor: فالطرف الكامل هو أن يكون بحيث يبذل كل ما يملكه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet says an angel calls each night for God to replace the spender's wealth and bring loss to the person who hoards it.
rows.anchor: وروي عنه صلى الله عليه وسلم أن الملك ينادي كل ليلة ( اللهم أعط كل منفق خلفا وكل ممسك تلفا )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hereafter's promise deserves trust over Satan's worldly poverty threat: the afterlife is certain, God's forgiveness is guaranteed, hoarded wealth may be unusable, worldly pleasure ends, and afterlife benefits are lasting and pure.
rows.anchor: وعد الرحمن في غد العقبى أولى بالقبول من وجوه أحدها : أن وجدان غد الدنيا مشكوك فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: مغفرة means erasure of sins, as in Q 9:103; its indefinite form and the phrase منه magnify it because the giver's greatness magnifies the gift.
rows.anchor: المراد بالمغفرة تكفير الذنوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exceptional forgiveness may turn sins into good deeds, make the donor an intercessor for other sinners, or include afterlife realities beyond present human understanding.
rows.anchor: كمال هذه المغفرة يحتمل أن يكون المراد منه ما قاله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: فضل can mean worldly recompense, but al-Rāzī prefers social goodwill: people helped by a generous person pray for and assist him, opening worldly good; he also explains psychological and spiritual benefits of giving.
rows.anchor: وهو أحسن الوجوه : أنه مهما عرف من الإنسان كونه منفقا لأمواله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse removes the suspicion that unbelievers benefit from spending on good works: their unbelief nullifies its reward, just as a cold wind destroys a crop.
rows.anchor: وحاصل الكلام أن كفرهم يبطل ثواب نفقتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent mismatch between spending and a destructive wind disappears if the analogy compares only the central outcome, a compound comparison rather than matching every component.
rows.anchor: المثل قسمان منه ما حصلت فيه المشابهة بين ما هو المقصود من الجملتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If components must correspond, one may supply the sense: unbelief destroys their spending, or their spending is like a destructive wind, or the phrase refers to funds spent to harm the Prophet and erase earlier good works.
rows.anchor: الأول : أن يكون التقدير : مثل الكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī's own proposed reading takes the spending as funds used against the Prophet; that unbelieving expenditure cancels earlier good works just as destructive wind cancels a crop.
rows.anchor: وهذا الوجه خطر ببالي عند كتابتي على هذا الموضع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spending may denote all deeds expected to benefit people in the afterlife, as other verses call deeds buying, selling, or spending; al-Rāzī prefers literal financial expenditure because the preceding verse mentions wealth and children.
rows.anchor: والقول الثاني : وهو الأشبه أن المراد إنفاق الأموال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report most strongly covers all unbelievers: worldly-directed spending leaves no afterlife benefit, while afterlife-directed spending cannot benefit them because unbelief bars its reward.
rows.anchor: المراد بالإخبار عن جميع الكفار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unbelievers may fund good works such as hospices, bridges, and aid for the vulnerable, yet find their charity erased by disbelief; this agrees with verses on deeds becoming dust, futile spending, mirage, and acceptance only from the God-fearing.
rows.anchor: ولعلهم أنفقوا أموالهم في الخيرات نحو بناء الرباطات والقناطر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If their expenditure funds sins such as harming the Messenger, killing Muslims, and destroying their homes, its failure is even more evident.
rows.anchor: أما إذا أنفقوها فيما ظنوه أنه الخيرات لكنه كان من المعاصي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The analogy may also describe worldly failure: unbelievers spend heavily to assemble armies and endure hardship, then Islam prevails, leaving them frustrated and regretful.
rows.anchor: فإنهم أنفقوا الأموال الكثيرة في جمع العساكر وتحملوا المشاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If only some unbelievers are meant, proposed groups are hypocrites giving from fear or accommodation, Abū Sufyān's party at Badr, lower-ranking Jews funding rabbis' distortions, or people whose supposed worship is mistaken.
rows.anchor: القول الثاني : المراد منه الإخبار عن بعض الكفار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة والسدي وابن زيد
rows.claim: Most exegetes and linguists, including Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, al-Suddī, and Ibn Zayd, take ṣirr as severe cold.
rows.anchor: قال أكثر المفسرين وأهل اللغة : الصر البرد الشديد

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الأصم وأبو بكر ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Abū Bakr al-Aṣamm and Ibn al-Anbārī interpret ṣirr as scorching heat or fire; Ibn al-Anbārī relates the sound of flames to the word, and both readings destroy crops.
rows.anchor: أن الصر : هو السموم الحارة والنار التي تغلي

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites infer reward cancellation from the crop analogy; al-Rāzī's school answers that reward depends on God's promise conditioned on faith, which unbelief removes, and earlier arguments against cancellation were given in al-Baqara.
rows.anchor: أجاب أصحابنا عنه بأن العمل لا يستلزم الثواب إلا بحكم الوعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ظلموا أنفسهم may mean they disobeyed and deserved their crop's destruction; unlike believers, whose sorrow can still increase their reward, unbelievers gain no worldly or afterlife benefit.
rows.anchor: أنهم عصوا الله فاستحقوا هلاك حرثهم عقوبة لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, they planted in the wrong place or season, since injustice is putting things out of place; their misplaced spending plus the misfortune of unbelief makes it fruitless.
rows.anchor: أن يكون المراد من قوله { ظلموا أنفسهم } هو أنهم زرعوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God did not wrong them by refusing their expenditure; they wronged themselves by attaching it to conditions that prevented divine acceptance.
rows.anchor: ما ظلمهم حيث لم يقبل نفقاتهم ، ولكنهم ظلموا أنفسهم

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf notes a doubled-lām reading of لكن; it means they wrong themselves, while dropping an implied subject pronoun is not permitted outside poetry.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) : قرىء { ولاكن } بالتشديد
